what: ESAB makes welding and cutting equipment and the consumables they use, such as welding wire, electrodes and gas regulators. It also sells gas control equipment for medical and industrial uses. It was spun out of Colfax (now Enovis) in 2022.
customers: Shipyards, construction firms, manufacturers of machinery, cars and energy equipment, and distributors that sell to small fabrication shops.
money: Wire, electrodes and other materials used up in every weld, bought again and again.
Welding machines, cutting systems and robotic welding cells.
Regulators and equipment for medical, industrial and specialty gases.
moat: A strong brand and global distribution, and a large share of revenue from consumables that customers keep buying, which makes sales steadier than those of pure equipment makers.
risks: Trailing net income of $157M is down from $227M in 2025, so profit is falling while revenue rises.
Debt of $2.5B against $2.6B of equity, and $2.7B of goodwill from acquisitions, leave little margin for error.
Welding demand follows industrial production and construction in Europe and the Americas, both sluggish recently.
Revenue has grown slowly, from $2.43B in 2021 to $2.84B in 2025.
opportunities: Trailing revenue of $3.1B is above any full year, helped by acquisitions in gas control.
The forward P/E of about 12.6, if analysts’ earnings estimates are right, is low for a business with this much recurring consumables revenue.
Eleven analysts average a target near $117, well above the price.
Infrastructure, shipbuilding and defense spending all need more welding.
watch: Whether earnings recover to the level analysts expect, which is what the low forward P/E assumes.
view: ESAB’s two P/E ratios tell opposite stories. On trailing earnings the stock trades at 30 times; on what analysts expect next year, about 12.6. The gap comes from charges and weaker margins that have cut reported profit from $227 million in 2025 to $157 million over the last twelve months, even as revenue rose to $3.1 billion.

The business underneath is sound: more than half of revenue is consumables, so a welder who buys an ESAB machine keeps buying ESAB wire for years. That is the same model that has made Lincoln Electric one of the steadiest industrial compounders, and ESAB trades at a large discount to it, partly because it carries more debt and more goodwill from deals.

So the question is which P/E is right. If the recent fall in profit reflects one-off costs from acquisitions and restructuring, the shares are cheap and the analysts’ target looks reasonable. If margins have structurally slipped, 30 times is a full price. I lean toward the first reading because cash flow has held up better than earnings, but I would want one or two quarters of recovering margins before believing the forward number.
bull: Margins recover, earnings reach the forward estimate and the shares close part of the gap to Lincoln Electric.
bear: The profit decline is structural, debt limits flexibility and the low forward P/E proves too optimistic.
